content.text: Good — cohort defined: **19,788 women** and **14,978 men** with dementia. Now I'll compute the top comorbidities per sex. I'll count distinct patients with each condition (excluding the dementia concepts themselves), normalize to prevalence within each sex, and rank.

arguments.sql_query:
WITH dem AS (
  SELECT ca.descendant_concept_id AS cid
  FROM omop.concept_ancestor ca
  WHERE ca.ancestor_concept_id = 4182210
),
cohort AS (
  SELECT p.person_id,
         CASE WHEN p.gender_concept_id = 8532 THEN 'FEMALE'
              WHEN p.gender_concept_id = 8507 THEN 'MALE' END AS sex
  FROM omop.person p
  WHERE p.gender_concept_id IN (8532, 8507)
    AND p.person_id IN (SELECT DISTINCT co.person_id FROM omop.condition_occurrence co WHERE co.condition_concept_id IN (SELECT cid FROM dem))
),
comorb AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT c.person_id, c.sex, co.condition_concept_id
  FROM cohort c
  JOIN omop.condition_occurrence co ON co.person_id = c.person_id
  WHERE co.condition_concept_id NOT IN (SELECT cid FROM dem)
    AND co.condition_concept_id <> 0
)
SELECT cm.sex, cm.condition_concept_id, cc.concept_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT cm.person_id) AS n_pts
FROM comorb cm
JOIN omop.concept cc ON cc.concept_id = cm.condition_concept_id
GROUP BY cm.sex, cm.condition_concept_id, cc.concept_name
ORDER BY cm.sex, n_pts DESC

The full ranking is too large to inline. Rather than re-query, I'll compute the ranked top comorbidities directly in SQL with sex-specific prevalence, so I get a compact comparison table. Let me run a focused query that returns the top conditions per sex with prevalence and a sex-difference metric.

arguments.sql_query:
WITH dem AS (
  SELECT ca.descendant_concept_id AS cid
  FROM omop.concept_ancestor ca
  WHERE ca.ancestor_concept_id = 4182210
),
cohort AS (
  SELECT p.person_id,
         CASE WHEN p.gender_concept_id = 8532 THEN 'F' ELSE 'M' END AS sex
  FROM omop.person p
  WHERE p.gender_concept_id IN (8532, 8507)
    AND p.person_id IN (SELECT DISTINCT co.person_id FROM omop.condition_occurrence co WHERE co.condition_concept_id IN (SELECT cid FROM dem))
),
denom AS (
  SELECT sex, COUNT(*) AS n FROM cohort GROUP BY sex
),
comorb AS (
  SELECT c.sex, co.condition_concept_id AS cid, COUNT(DISTINCT c.person_id) AS n_pts
  FROM cohort c
  JOIN omop.condition_occurrence co ON co.person_id = c.person_id
  WHERE co.condition_concept_id NOT IN (SELECT cid FROM dem) AND co.condition_concept_id <> 0
  GROUP BY c.sex, co.condition_concept_id
),
pivot AS (
  SELECT cid,
    SUM(CASE WHEN sex='F' THEN n_pts ELSE 0 END) AS f_pts,
    SUM(CASE WHEN sex='M' THEN n_pts ELSE 0 END) AS m_pts
  FROM comorb GROUP BY cid
),
fd AS (SELECT n AS fn FROM denom WHERE sex='F'),
md AS (SELECT n AS mn FROM denom WHERE sex='M')
SELECT TOP 40 cc.concept_name,
  p.f_pts, CAST(100.0*p.f_pts/fd.fn AS DECIMAL(5,1)) AS f_pct,
  p.m_pts, CAST(100.0*p.m_pts/md.mn AS DECIMAL(5,1)) AS m_pct,
  CAST(100.0*p.f_pts/fd.fn - 100.0*p.m_pts/md.mn AS DECIMAL(5,1)) AS f_minus_m_pct
FROM pivot p CROSS JOIN fd CROSS JOIN md
JOIN omop.concept cc ON cc.concept_id = p.cid
WHERE (p.f_pts + p.m_pts) >= 500
ORDER BY (p.f_pts + p.m_pts) DESC

WITH dem AS (
  SELECT ca.descendant_concept_id AS cid
  FROM omop.concept_ancestor ca
  WHERE ca.ancestor_concept_id = 4182210
),
cohort AS (
  SELECT p.person_id,
         CASE WHEN p.gender_concept_id = 8532 THEN 'F' ELSE 'M' END AS sex
  FROM omop.person p
  WHERE p.gender_concept_id IN (8532, 8507)
    AND p.person_id IN (SELECT DISTINCT co.person_id FROM omop.condition_occurrence co WHERE co.condition_concept_id IN (SELECT cid FROM dem))
),
denom AS (
  SELECT sex, COUNT(*) AS n FROM cohort GROUP BY sex
),
comorb AS (
  SELECT c.sex, co.condition_concept_id AS cid, COUNT(DISTINCT c.person_id) AS n_pts
  FROM cohort c
  JOIN omop.condition_occurrence co ON co.person_id = c.person_id
  WHERE co.condition_concept_id NOT IN (SELECT cid FROM dem) AND co.condition_concept_id <> 0
  GROUP BY c.sex, co.condition_concept_id
),
wide AS (
  SELECT cid,
    SUM(CASE WHEN sex='F' THEN n_pts ELSE 0 END) AS f_pts,
    SUM(CASE WHEN sex='M' THEN n_pts ELSE 0 END) AS m_pts
  FROM comorb GROUP BY cid
),
fd AS (SELECT n AS fn FROM denom WHERE sex='F'),
md AS (SELECT n AS mn FROM denom WHERE sex='M')
SELECT TOP 45 cc.concept_name,
  w.f_pts, CAST(100.0*w.f_pts/fd.fn AS DECIMAL(5,1)) AS f_pct,
  w.m_pts, CAST(100.0*w.m_pts/md.mn AS DECIMAL(5,1)) AS m_pct,
  CAST(100.0*w.f_pts/fd.fn - 100.0*w.m_pts/md.mn AS DECIMAL(5,1)) AS f_minus_m_pct
FROM wide w CROSS JOIN fd CROSS JOIN md
JOIN omop.concept cc ON cc.concept_id = w.cid
WHERE (w.f_pts + w.m_pts) >= 500
ORDER BY (w.f_pts + w.m_pts) DESC

## Cohort
Patients with any dementia (SNOMED "Dementia" + all descendants) at our center: **19,788 women** and **14,978 men**. Comorbidity = distinct patients with each condition concept, as % of that sex's dementia cohort.

## Comorbidities shared by both sexes (the backbone)
Cardiometabolic and general-illness conditions dominate for everyone with dementia:

| Condition | Women % | Men % |
|---|---|---|
| Essential hypertension | 52.8 | 50.1 |
| Hyperlipidemia | 38.3 | 39.8 |
| Anemia | 29.0 | 29.8 |
| Depressive disorder | 24.4 | 20.7 |
| Type 2 diabetes | 17.4 | 19.2 |
| Atrial fibrillation | 18.2 | 21.0 |
| Congestive heart failure | 16.0 | 16.6 |

## Where the sexes diverge (prevalence difference, women − men)

**Higher in women with dementia:**
| Condition | Women % | Men % | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Osteoporosis | 23.7 | 6.7 | **+17.0** |
| Urinary tract infection | 32.0 | 20.1 | **+11.9** |
| Hypothyroidism | 20.8 | 11.2 | **+9.7** |
| Osteoarthritis | 18.3 | 10.6 | +7.7 |
| Disorder of bone | 15.7 | 9.4 | +6.3 |
| Headache | 15.4 | 10.7 | +4.7 |
| Depressive disorder | 24.4 | 20.7 | +3.7 |

**Higher in men with dementia:**
| Condition | Women % | Men % | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coronary atherosclerosis (no angina) | 10.3 | 17.4 | **−7.2** |
| Acute kidney injury | 18.2 | 22.8 | −4.7 |
| Chronic kidney disease | 12.9 | 17.4 | −4.4 |
| Low blood pressure | 11.6 | 15.1 | −3.4 |
| Cardiac arrhythmia | 11.9 | 14.7 | −2.8 |
| Atrial fibrillation | 18.2 | 21.0 | −2.8 |
| Pneumonia / sepsis | ~14 | ~16 | −2 to −3 |

## Plausible biological underpinnings

**Female-predominant patterns**
- **Osteoporosis / osteoarthritis / bone disorders (largest gap):** post-menopausal estrogen loss accelerates bone resorption; estrogen also modulates cartilage and joint tissue. Reduced estrogen after menopause is the dominant mechanism, compounded by lower peak bone mass and longer survival into old age in women.
- **UTI:** shorter female urethra and peri-urethral colonization, plus post-menopausal urogenital atrophy (loss of estrogen-dependent vaginal *Lactobacillus* and mucosal defense) raise ascending-infection risk — amplified in dementia by incontinence and reduced fluid intake.
- **Hypothyroidism:** autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroid disease is several-fold more common in women, an X-linked/sex-hormone-influenced autoimmune predisposition; overlap of hypothyroid cognitive slowing with dementia may also increase ascertainment.
- **Depression:** consistent female preponderance across life, tied to HPA-axis and gonadal-hormone reactivity plus differential reporting/ascertainment.

**Male-predominant patterns**
- **Coronary atherosclerosis, arrhythmia, AF, CKD/AKI:** men develop atherosclerotic vascular disease earlier (women are relatively protected pre-menopause by estrogen's favorable lipid/endothelial effects). This vascular burden plausibly reflects a **larger vascular contribution to their dementia** — consistent with the higher rates of coronary disease and renal vascular injury, and pointing toward vascular/mixed rather than purely neurodegenerative etiology in men.
- **Pneumonia/sepsis, hypotension:** may reflect later-stage or more medically fragile presentation and sex differences in immune response.

## Important caveats
- These are **observational EHR prevalences, not adjusted rates.** Women in the cohort are more numerous and typically older at dementia diagnosis (they live longer), so age confounds several differences (osteoporosis, UTI especially).
- Many concepts are **symptoms/findings** ("chest pain," "abnormal ECG," "impaired cognition"), not clean diagnoses — reflecting documentation, not just disease.
- Diagnostic **ascertainment differs by sex** (e.g., women screened more for osteoporosis/thyroid), inflating some gaps.
- Dementia subtype is not separated here; the male vascular-comorbidity signal would be worth confirming by stratifying Alzheimer vs. vascular dementia.
